overview.text: Radiometric dating is a family of methods for estimating the numeric ages of rocks, minerals, and some once-living materials. Radioactive isotopes—atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons—decay at predictable rates, turning into daughter isotopes. By measuring the proportions of parent and daughter isotopes and applying the isotope’s half-life, scientists estimate when the material or a geologic event formed. Different isotope pairs suit different materials and timescales: potassium-argon can date volcanic rocks, while carbon-14 is used for relatively recent organic remains, not rocks themselves. These dates help reconstruct Earth’s history, but the result depends on the material and geological context; sedimentary rocks can be especially difficult to date directly.

key_facts.text: An isotope’s half-life is the time required for half of a sample’s radioactive parent atoms to decay.
Geologists commonly use uranium-lead and potassium-argon dating; different isotope pairs are useful across different timescales.
Carbon-14 dating estimates the age of suitable organic material; it does not directly date rocks.
A date from igneous rock minerals generally records when they crystallized; a date from metamorphic minerals may record mineral formation or later cooling.
Sedimentary rocks can be harder to date because their grains may have formed before the sediment was deposited; dated ash layers can help constrain their age.
